Every mapped datacentre on Earth

5,280 map objects carrying a datacentre tag, as mapped in OpenStreetMap on 2026-10-03

Where anybody has written a datacentre into OpenStreetMap — a public, openly-licensed map that anyone can read and anyone can edit — attributed to a country and counted. The United States map on this site joins each of its pins to the water and the grid around it; no such join exists for the rest of the planet, so this page joins nothing. It draws, it attributes, and it counts.

5,280 datacentres, as mapped in OpenStreetMap on 2026-10-03. That is the number of map objects, and it is not the number of datacentres in the world. A country with no mapped datacentre is a country nobody has mapped. It is not a country with no datacentres, and this data cannot tell those two apart.

  • 5,280 datacentres mapped as mapped in OpenStreetMap on 2026-10-03. Not a count of datacentres that exist.
  • 113 countries with a site of 237 in the roster. The other 124 have none mapped, which means nobody has mapped them.
  • 5,121 operating a datacentre tag with no construction, proposed or planned qualifier
  • 119 under construction a construction tag, in OpenStreetMap
  • 40 announced a proposed or planned tag; located to the evidence, never more precisely
  • 38.7% in the United States 2,041 sites. Not the same count as /map, which keeps only what it can place in a county.
  • 79 in no country polygon published as unresolved, never guessed. Drawn on the map where the coordinate is, with no country in the popup.

Read this before you read the map

A country with no mapped datacentre is a country nobody has mapped. It is not a country with no datacentres, and this data cannot tell those two apart.

Every figure on this page counts map objects carrying a datacentre tag in OpenStreetMap on 2026-10-03. Coverage follows volunteers, not deployments: a dense country is a country somebody mapped, and comparing two countries here is partly comparing how many people were looking.

This page joins nothing; it counts. The United States figure here is not the figure on the United States map, which keeps only the sites it can place in a county and joins them to drought, grid and river data. Both numbers are printed, and neither is adjusted toward the other.

The map 5,280

One pin per mapped site, drawn exactly where OpenStreetMap places the object. The picture needs no JavaScript and every figure in it is a number in the table below. With it, the map pans and zooms, and hovering or tapping a pin names the site, its operator, its status and its place — or says which of those OpenStreetMap does not record.

Below 760 pixels the map is drawn only once the script has wired up pinch and zoom: 5,280 pins on a 343-pixel picture is a smudge, and a smudge that cannot be read still looks authoritative. The table below carries every channel the map encodes except position.

Shape is status

  • operating 5,121
  • under construction 119
  • announced 40

Distinguishable in greyscale and in a screenshot. Status is read from the OpenStreetMap tag that set it: a construction tag is under construction, a proposed or planned tag is announced, anything else with a datacentre tag is operating. Every pin carries its status in the JSON.

Colour is one colour

  • every pin 5,280

On the United States map colour is the drought in the pin's county and size is its tagged capacity. Neither join exists outside the United States, so here every pin is the same size and the same colour, and nothing is being said by either. A pin is 2.4 units across and is drawn exactly where OpenStreetMap places the object.

What is not drawn

  • Antarctica 0
  • no outline, pins drawn 107
  • no country resolved 79
  • outside the frame 0

Antarctica carries no mapped datacentre and the frame stops at 57° south, so it is left off rather than drawn empty. 7 countries with a mapped site have no outline at the 1:110m scale drawn here — Singapore (92), Hong Kong S.A.R. (6), Bahrain (4), Isle of Man (2), Curaçao (1), Faroe Islands (1), Mauritius (1) — so their 107 pins sit on what looks like sea. They are in the table with a note. 79 pins fell inside no country polygon and are drawn without a country: the popup says so, and they have no row in the country table but one row of their own at its foot. Every site with a coordinate fell inside the drawn frame; a site outside it would be listed here in words rather than dragged to the edge.

Computing hardware in orbitOff the planet 23

There are no data centres in space. On the as-of date, hardware in orbit that could be called compute totals a few dozen spacecraft; the constellations filed with regulators total more than a million. A register that printed only the filed number would be repeating a press release.

23 spacecraft in orbit carrying compute hardware on 2026-09-27, against 1,142,481 satellites filed or planned for it — 49,673 on paper for every one flying — and a further 193,428 filed with the purpose unstated. The two numbers are printed together everywhere on this page, because the second one printed alone is a press release.

  • 23 spacecraft in orbit carrying compute hardware, counted once — a hosted payload is not a second spacecraft
  • 1,142,481 filed or planned for compute the sum of the programmes’ own filings and stated targets. Numbers on paper.
  • 49,673 filed for every one flying the second counter divided by the first
  • 193,428 filed, purpose unstated listed with the purpose left blank rather than assigned to orbital compute
  • announced 5
  • awaiting-launch 1
  • demonstrated 2
  • operating 3
  • study 2
  • unclear 2

Every programme in the register, in the register's own order. In orbit now is hardware in space on the as-of date; claimed or filed is the programme's own number, on paper. They sit in adjacent columns so neither is read without the other. Sources are numbered links; the row says where its sources disagree.

A register of every programme that claims, files for, or has flown computing hardware in orbit or on the Moon described as a data centre. Each row separates what is actually in space from what has been announced or filed, with the sources for both.

What the register can and cannot say

  • Every date, count and figure below is taken from a linked source; where sources disagree the row says so. Nothing is estimated.
  • in_orbit_spacecraft counts spacecraft carrying compute hardware that is in space on the as-of date. Hosted payloads on another programme's satellites are not counted twice: Axiom's two nodes ride on Kepler's ten.
  • filed_or_planned_satellites is the number in the programme's own filing or stated target. It is a number on paper. It is printed beside the flown number so it cannot be read alone.
  • Statuses change at launch. A launch is not commissioning and commissioning is not first inference; a row moves to operating only when a source reports the hardware working.
  • Programmes with unverified purpose (CTC-1/2, Space Compass) are listed with their purpose left blank rather than assigned to orbital compute.

What this can and cannot say

A country with no mapped datacentre is a country nobody has mapped. It is not a country with no datacentres, and this data cannot tell those two apart.

Published by the collector, printed here unedited.

  • Every figure counts map objects carrying a datacentre tag in OpenStreetMap on 2026-10-03. It is not a count of datacentres that exist.
  • Status is read from the tags: a construction tag is under construction, a proposed or planned tag is announced, anything else with a datacentre tag is operating. A tag that has not been updated since a building opened is still "under construction" here.
  • Countries are assigned by point-in-polygon against Natural Earth 1:50m outlines, generalised to about 1 km. 25 sites sit within about 2 km of a border and could belong to the neighbour. 79 sites fall in no polygon and are published as unresolved rather than guessed.
  • Coverage follows volunteers, not deployments. A dense country is a country somebody mapped; a blank one may simply not have been mapped.
  • The United States figure here differs from /map, which keeps only the sites it can place in a county and joins them to drought, grid and river data. This page joins nothing; it counts.
  • 0 elements arrived without a usable coordinate and were dropped; 0 carried no tags.

How each site got its country. 5,196 sites were placed by point-in-polygon; 5 fell in no polygon and were placed by their own addr:country tag; 79 had neither and are published as unresolved. 1 site carries an addr:country tag that disagrees with the polygon it fell in; the polygon wins and the disagreement is flagged in the JSON. 7 countries with a mapped site have no outline at the 1:110m scale this map is drawn at — the attribution used the 1:50m file, which has them — so their pins are drawn over sea. This is a snapshot and not a time series: nothing here says when a datacentre opened or whether anything runs in it, only that an OpenStreetMap object with the tag exists.

Where this came from

OpenStreetMap via Overpass, worldwide. One planet-wide query against https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter, keyless, for 16 tag variants; 5,280 elements came back in 1,816 KiB, 0 without a usable coordinate and 0 without tags. OpenStreetMap's own snapshot clock for this extract reads 2026-10-03T16:47:01Z; this file was generated 2026-10-03 17:29:44 UTC (cache, refreshed every 7 days).

The query

Sent as the data= field of a GET, which Overpass accepts identically to a form-encoded POST. Every figure on this page is arithmetic over the response.

[out:json][timeout:600];
(
  nwr["telecom"="data_center"];
  nwr["telecom"="data_centre"];
  nwr["building"="data_center"];
  nwr["building:use"="data_center"];
  nwr["industrial"="data_centre"];
  nwr["industrial"="data_center"];
  nwr["industrial"="datacenter"];
  nwr["man_made"="data_center"];
  nwr["construction:telecom"="data_center"];
  nwr["construction"="data_center"];
  nwr["construction"="datacenter"];
  nwr["construction"="data_centre"];
  nwr["proposed:telecom"="data_center"];
  nwr["proposed:building"="data_center"];
  nwr["planned:telecom"="data_center"];
  nwr["planned:industrial"="datacenter"];
);
out tags center qt;

The 16 tag variants, unioned: telecom=data_center telecom=data_centre building=data_center building:use=data_center industrial=data_centre industrial=data_center industrial=datacenter man_made=data_center construction:telecom=data_center construction=data_center construction=datacenter construction=data_centre proposed:telecom=data_center proposed:building=data_center planned:telecom=data_center planned:industrial=datacenter

Geography

Countries were assigned against Natural Earth 1:50m admin-0 countries (v5.1.2), 242 polygons, public domain, read from cache 0 days old and refreshed every 90 days. country polygons generalised to about 1 km; a site within about a kilometre of a land border can be assigned to the neighbour, and says so. The border flag steps 0.02 degrees out in eight directions and checks whether any of them lands in a different country. A site in no polygon is published as unresolved.

The outlines drawn above are a different, coarser file: Natural Earth, 1:110m Admin 0 - Countries (ne_110m_admin_0_countries.geojson), public domain, retrieved 2026-09-27 — 177 countries, 287 rings, 5,481 vertices after simplification by visvalingam-whyatt, minimum triangle 0.2 deg², coordinates quantised to 0.01°. Drawing is not attribution: a pin's country came from the finer file, and the coarser one is only the picture under it. Made with Natural Earth. Take the data

Published beside this page byte-identical to the committed files — the build copies them verbatim rather than re-serialising, so the checksum of the file in the repository is the checksum of the file served here.

  • /api/world.json Every number on this page: the totals, all 5,280 sites with coordinate, status, name, operator, city and country, the 113 country rows, the copy block and the honesty list. OpenStreetMap data, ODbL.
  • /api/orbital.json The orbital register: 15 programmes, each with what is in space, what is filed, and the sources for both.

AI Early Warning System

Detected early, not a prediction. We count.

DOOMCON measures how much is happening, not how bad it is. Levels run from 5 (quietest) to 1 (loudest) and describe observable activity tempo against this index’s own record. They are not a probability of harm.

Datacentre locations on this page are © OpenStreetMap contributors, licensed under the Open Database License. A country with no mapped datacentre is a country nobody has mapped. It is not a country with no datacentres, and this data cannot tell those two apart.

Collection runs on a published */15 cron; scheduled runs are queued and are routinely late, which is why the rail above says overdue rather than counting down into fiction. Every value on this site is computed from public data by published code, and each observation is written to a hash-chained receipt carrying its full inputs — so anyone can recompute the number and get the same answer.
